title: Milestone: How People Build
objective: After this level you can connect materials, climate and purpose into one picture of architecture.
summary: Rudofsky's 1964 MoMA show celebrated architecture without architects. Snow, earth, felt, stilts and timber each answer a climate with Chapter 1's physics.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. So who designed all these homes?
cards.body: Igloos, gers, adobe pueblos, stilt houses: most of this chapter's homes are what ICOMOS calls vernacular building, "the traditional and natural way by which communities house themselves." In 1964, an architect put that idea on the walls of a famous museum.

cards.headline: Architecture Without Architects
cards.body: That was the title of an exhibition at New York's Museum of Modern Art, opening in November 1964. Its director, the architect and engineer Bernard Rudofsky, called his subject non-pedigreed architecture: old, sometimes ancient building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people. Level 1 said architects design and builders build. Rudofsky's point: whole communities can do both.

cards.headline: One problem, one answer, one piece of physics

items.label: Cold: the Inuit igloo
points: Compressed snow insulates better than ice
Tiered floors put sleepers in the warmest air

items.label: Earth and felt: adobe and the ger
points: Thick earth stores heat, so rooms peak hours later
A yurt's center ring squeezes; a band around the wall pulls

items.label: Water and wood: stilts and frames
points: Rumah panggung let floods flow beneath the floor
Timber frames carry the load; infill keeps out the weather

questions.prompt: What did Bernard Rudofsky call the building traditions in his 1964 MoMA exhibition?

options.label: Non-pedigreed architecture
Primitive architecture
options.rationale: Rudofsky's own term was non-pedigreed.

options.label: The International Style
options.rationale: That's a modernist style, not his subject.

options.label: Firmness, commodity and delight
options.rationale: That's Vitruvius's triad from Level 1.

questions.explanation: Rudofsky's own term for his subject was non-pedigreed architecture.

questions.prompt: Level 1's architect designs and hands builders drawings. What did 'Architecture Without Architects' celebrate instead?

options.label: Buildings designed by computers
options.rationale: The show was about human building traditions.

options.label: Traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people
Only the grandest palaces and temples
options.rationale: It celebrated non-pedigreed, everyday building.

options.label: Buildings with no drawings or plans ever made
options.rationale: Its focus was who built them: ordinary people.

questions.explanation: Rudofsky's exhibition presented old building traditions evolved and upheld by ordinary people, rather than works by named architects.

questions.prompt: How Homes Are Built milestone: why do some igloos have tiered floors?

options.label: So snow blocks can be stored indoors
options.rationale: The tiers are about warmth.

options.label: So people can sleep up high, where it's warmer
So the lamp can sit below the floor
options.rationale: The lamp is in the living space.

options.label: So the dome can rise without a frame
options.rationale: That's the spiral, not the floors.

questions.explanation: Some igloos have tiered floors so people can sleep above the lowest level, where it is warmer.

questions.prompt: How Homes Are Built milestone: in a yurt roof, which part is held in compression?

options.label: The band around the top of the wall
options.rationale: That band is in tension.

options.label: The felt covers
options.rationale: The covers carry no structural squeeze.

options.label: The center ring where the roof poles meet
The ropes of animal hair
options.rationale: Ropes pull; they're in tension.

questions.explanation: The roof poles meet in a center ring that holds them in compression; the band at the wall top is in tension.

questions.prompt: How Homes Are Built milestone: what does high thermal mass mean for a thick earth wall?

options.label: It can store a lot of heat and release it slowly
It reflects sunlight like a mirror
options.rationale: Thermal mass is about storing heat.

options.label: It lets cool air flow straight through
options.rationale: The wall stores heat; it doesn't vent.

options.label: It weighs too much to need foundations
options.rationale: Mass here means stored heat, not skipping foundations.

questions.explanation: Thermal mass is a material's ability to store heat; thick earth walls soak heat up slowly, so the room peaks a few hours after the outside.

questions.prompt: How Homes Are Built milestone: besides letting floods pass, what does the open space under a rumah panggung do?

options.label: It stores snow for building blocks
options.rationale: That's the Arctic, not Sumatra.

options.label: It holds the house's tension band
options.rationale: That's a yurt's wall.

options.label: It traps warm air like an igloo's platform
options.rationale: The space is open for air to flow.

options.label: It lets in air and light, cutting damp that rots wood

questions.explanation: The open space beneath the floor lets in air and light, reducing the humidity that damages the wooden structure.

questions.prompt: How Homes Are Built milestone: which Chapter 1 idea lets a timber house get away with walls of mud and straw?

options.label: An arch's thrust at its feet
options.rationale: No arch here; it's a frame.

options.label: A frame carries the load, so infill holds only itself
A dome's hoop forces
options.rationale: Domes aren't involved in timber framing.

options.label: Stone's strength in compression
options.rationale: The point is that the frame carries the load.

questions.explanation: In a frame building, the skeleton carries the floors and the wall bears only its own weight; the timber frame does the carrying, so the infill needs only to keep out the weather.
